<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
Let $z_1,\ldots,z_5\in\mathbb C$ satisfy
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^5|z_j|^2=5.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mainineq}
 \prod_{1\le i<j\le5}|z_i-z_j|^2\le5^5.
\end{equation}
Equality holds if and only if, after a permutation,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equalitycase}
 z_j=e^{\mathrm i\theta}\omega^{j-1},
 \qquad
 \omega=e^{2\pi\mathrm i/5},
 \qquad j=1,\ldots,5,
\end{equation}
for some $\theta\in\mathbb R$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:maxexists}
The maximum $M_n$ in \eqref{eq:defDelta} exists.  Every maximizer with positive value is collision-free.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The set $\{z\in\mathbb C^n:Q(z)=n\}$ is compact and $\Delta_n$ is continuous, so a maximum exists.  A regular $n$-gon has positive product.  Hence a maximizer cannot contain two equal points.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:equilibrium}
Every maximizer in Theorem~\ref{thm:main} satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equilibrium}
 \sum_{j\ne i}\frac1{z_i-z_j}=2\overline{z_i},
 \qquad i=1,\ldots,5.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:centroid}
 \sum_{i=1}^5z_i=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Wirtinger differentiation gives
\[
 \frac{\partial L}{\partial\overline z_i}
 =\sum_{j\ne i}\frac1{\overline z_i-\overline z_j}.
\]
Thus there is a real multiplier $\lambda$ such that
\[
 \sum_{j\ne i}\frac1{z_i-z_j}=\lambda\overline z_i.
\]
Multiplying by $z_i$ and summing over $i$ yields
\[
 \lambda\sum_i|z_i|^2
 =\sum_{i<j}\left(\frac{z_i}{z_i-z_j}
   +\frac{z_j}{z_j-z_i}\right)=10.
\]
Since $Q(z)=5$, we have $\lambda=2$, proving \eqref{eq:equilibrium}.  Summing \eqref{eq:equilibrium} over $i$ gives $2\sum_i\overline z_i=0$, because the terms on the left cancel in pairs.  This gives \eqref{eq:centroid}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:mixedmoments}
Every collision-free solution of \eqref{eq:complexified} satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mixedmoments}
 \sum_i x_i\xi_i^2=0,
 \qquad
 \sum_i x_i\xi_i^3=7\sum_i\xi_i^2,
 \qquad
 \sum_i x_i\xi_i^4=6\sum_i\xi_i^3.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the coefficients in \eqref{eq:R0coeff}--\eqref{eq:RTcoeff} satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:threeeqs}
 s_2=0,
 \qquad
 s_1=6r_3,
 \qquad
 s_0=2r_2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Multiply \eqref{eq:xi-second} by $\xi_i^m$ and sum over $i$.  Pairing the terms indexed by $i,j$ gives
\[
 \sum_i\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{\xi_i^m}{\xi_i-\xi_j}
 =\sum_{i<j}\frac{\xi_i^m-\xi_j^m}{\xi_i-\xi_j}.
\]
For $m=2$, this is $(5-1)\sum_i\xi_i=0$.  For $m=3$, it equals
\[
 4\sum_i\xi_i^2+\sum_{i<j}\xi_i\xi_j
 =\frac72\sum_i\xi_i^2,
\]
because $\sum_i\xi_i=0$.  For $m=4$, it equals
\[
 4\sum_i\xi_i^3
 +\sum_{i<j}(\xi_i^2\xi_j+\xi_i\xi_j^2)
 =3\sum_i\xi_i^3.
\]
Comparison with the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:xi-second} gives \eqref{eq:mixedmoments}.  Expanding \eqref{eq:Rproduct} and applying Newton identities converts these three equalities into \eqref{eq:threeeqs}.  The conversion is also reconstructed symbolically in the verification script.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:reflection}
Every collision-free physical solution of \eqref{eq:equilibrium} is invariant under reflection in some line through the origin.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:genericelim}
The ideal \eqref{eq:Isat} is the intersection of the following two zero-dimensional ideals:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:decomp}
 \mathcal I
 =\langle P_1,c-C_1,k-K_1\rangle
 \cap
 \langle P_2,c-C_2,k-K_2\rangle,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{align}
 P_1(B)&=125B^4+7900B^3-37040B^2+44608B+512,\label{eq:P1}\\
 P_2(B)&=2500B^4-114000B^3+338925B^2-11000B+6912,\label{eq:P2}
\end{align}
and
\begin{align}
 C_1(B)&=\frac{3(125B^3+8020B^2-16496B+4224)}{57088},\label{eq:C1}\\
 K_1(B)&=\frac{75B^3+4812B^2-16320B+13952}{28544},\label{eq:K1}\\
 C_2(B)&=-\frac{1250B^3-69425B^2+327305B-145296}{443535},\label{eq:C2}\\
 K_2(B)&=-\frac{28500B^3-1287200B^2+3884705B-1798816}{5913800}.\label{eq:K2}
\end{align}
The factors $P_1$ and $P_2$ are coprime and $P_1P_2$ is square-free.  In addition, on $\mathcal I$ one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dualinvariants}
 \delta r_2^2=b^2r_3^3,
 \qquad
 \delta r_1=cr_3^2,
 \qquad
 \delta r_0=kr_3r_2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
All assertions are identities over $\mathbb Q$.  The saturation is computed by the Rabinowitsch trick: introduce $s$ and compute a Gr\"obner basis of
\[
 \langle F_1,F_2,F_3,sB\widetilde\delta-1\rangle
 \subset\mathbb Q[s,k,c,B].
\]
A change to lexicographic order gives a triangular zero-dimensional basis whose eliminant is the monic form of $P_1P_2$; reduction modulo $P_j$ gives precisely \eqref{eq:C1}--\eqref{eq:K2}.  Exact polynomial division verifies the two inclusions in \eqref{eq:decomp}, the coprimality and square-freeness assertions, and zero normal form for each numerator in \eqref{eq:dualinvariants}.  Appendix~\ref{app:generic} gives the input polynomials, and the accompanying verification script reconstructs the resultant \eqref{eq:resultant} from scratch and performs every division over $\mathbb Q$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:exceptional}
For a collision-free physical solution:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item If $a\ne0$ and $b=0$, then after normalizing $a=1$,
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:exceptional1}
  d=0,
  \qquad
  c=\frac3{20}.
 \end{equation}
 Hence $p(X)=X^5+X^3+\frac3{20}X$, whose roots lie on a line.
 \item The chart $a=0$, $b\ne0$ contains no physical solution.
 \item If $a=b=0$, then $cd=0$.  Thus, up to scaling,
 \[
  p(X)=X^5+cX
  \quad\text{or}\quad
  p(X)=X^5+d,
 \]
 corresponding to the centered square or a regular pentagon.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Normalize $a=1$ in the first case and $b=1$ in the second.  The saturated lexicographic bases are, respectively,
\[
 \left\{s-\frac{3125}{27},\ d,\ c-\frac3{20}\right\},
 \qquad
 \{1\}.
\]
In the third case, the $s$-free part of the saturated basis is generated by $cd$.  These are exact Gr\"obner-basis computations over $\mathbb Q$ and are reproduced in Appendix~\ref{app:generic} and in the verification script.  Finally,
\[
 X^5+X^3+\frac3{20}X
 =X\left(X^4+X^2+\frac3{20}\right),
\]
and both roots of the quadratic equation in $X^2$ are negative real numbers; hence all five roots are collinear after rotation.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The generic case follows from \eqref{eq:Breal} and the discussion after it.  Proposition~\ref{prop:exceptional} treats all remaining coefficient charts.  A monic polynomial with real coefficients has a root set invariant under complex conjugation.  Undoing the common rotation gives reflection symmetry about a line through the origin.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:one-real-elim}
A lexicographic Gr\"obner basis of \eqref{eq:remainders}--\eqref{eq:remq2} contains
\begin{equation}\label{eq:etaepsilon-rel}
 2\eta\varepsilon=5h(h^2-1),
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:eta2-rel}
 h\bigl(276\eta^2+2450h^8-14875h^6+28975h^4
 -16475h^2-1455\bigr)=0,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:elim-h}
 h(h^2-1)
 \bigl(10h^8-65h^6+140h^4-97h^2+6\bigr)=0.
\end{equation}
The complete six-element basis is given in Appendix~\ref{app:symmetric}.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Expand \eqref{eq:remainders} and take the two coefficients of each of the linear remainders in \eqref{eq:remq1}--\eqref{eq:remq2}.  Exact Buchberger reduction over $\mathbb Q$ gives the basis displayed in Appendix~\ref{app:symmetric}; the last, second, and fifth elements yield \eqref{eq:etaepsilon-rel}--\eqref{eq:elim-h}.  The verification script constructs these five equations directly from \eqref{eq:factor12}--\eqref{eq:vepsilon} and checks the basis.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:32}
The equations \eqref{eq:32remainders} imply
\begin{equation}\label{eq:u32}
 u\bigl(10u^8-55u^6+115u^4-37u^2-9\bigr)=0.
\end{equation}
If $u=0$, they give $C=0$ and $v=5/4$, hence the centered square.  If $u\ne0$ and $U=u^2$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Q32}
 10U^4-55U^3+115U^2-37U-9=0
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:V32}
 v=-\frac{130U^3-625U^2+1074U-211}{304}.
\end{equation}
The polynomial in \eqref{eq:Q32} has exactly one positive root, lying in
\[
 0.607600<U<0.607601,
\]
and \eqref{eq:V32} is negative throughout this interval.  Consequently the $u\ne0$ branch cannot contain a nonreal conjugate pair.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The exact lexicographic basis is displayed in Appendix~\ref{app:symmetric}.  Its last element is \eqref{eq:u32}; the remaining elements give \eqref{eq:V32}.  Sturm's theorem proves the asserted positive-root count, and direct rational interval evaluation proves $v<0$.  If $q$ had a nonreal conjugate pair, then $v$ would be the squared modulus of either root and hence positive, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:collinear}
The unique monic degree-five solution of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:HermiteODE}
 p''-4Xp'+20p=0
\end{equation}
with zero $X^4$ coefficient is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:collinearpoly}
 p(X)=X^5-\frac52X^3+\frac{15}{16}X.
\end{equation}
Its roots are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:collinearroots}
 0,
 \qquad
 \pm\sqrt{\frac{5+\sqrt{10}}4},
 \qquad
 \pm\sqrt{\frac{5-\sqrt{10}}4}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Substitution of a general monic quintic with no $X^4$ term into \eqref{eq:HermiteODE} determines the remaining coefficients uniquely and gives \eqref{eq:collinearpoly}.  Factoring the even quartic after removing the root $0$ gives \eqref{eq:collinearroots}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:classification}
Up to rotation and permutation, the collision-free physical solutions of \eqref{eq:equilibrium} consist of exactly five configurations:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item the regular pentagon;
 \item the centered square;
 \item the collinear configuration \eqref{eq:collinearroots};
 \item the two nonclassical configurations $E_-$ and $E_+$ determined exactly by \eqref{eq:QH}--\eqref{eq:epsilonH} with $H=H_-$ and $H=H_+$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:maxexists}, a global maximizer exists and is collision-free.  Proposition~\ref{prop:equilibrium} shows that it satisfies \eqref{eq:equilibrium}.  Theorem~\ref{thm:classification} therefore restricts it to the five configurations listed above.  Equations \eqref{eq:pentdisc}--\eqref{eq:Dintervals} show that the regular pentagon is the unique maximizing shape.  Its moment is $5$, so its circumradius is $1$.  This gives \eqref{eq:equalitycase} and completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:fekete}
The global maximizers of \eqref{eq:weightedV} are, up to permutation and common rotation,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weightedpent}
 z_j=\sqrt2\,e^{2\pi\mathrm i(j-1)/5},
 \qquad j=1,\ldots,5.
\end{equation}
The maximum value is
\[
 2^{10}5^5e^{-10}.
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
For a nonzero configuration $z$ and $r>0$,
\[
 \mathcal G(rz)=r^{20}e^{-r^2Q(z)}\Delta_5(z).
\]
Along each ray this is maximized at $r^2Q(z)=10$.  Rescale the resulting configuration by $1/\sqrt2$; it then has moment $5$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:main} applies.  Conversely \eqref{eq:weightedpent} attains the stated value.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:ginibre}
The symmetric joint density \eqref{eq:ginibre-density} on the labeled space
$\mathbb C^5$ is maximized precisely by the labeled regular pentagons of radius
$\sqrt2$ centered at the origin.  Equivalently, its pushforward to the
unordered configuration space $\mathbb C^5/S_5$, with the induced quotient measure,
has the regular-pentagon orbit as its unique global mode up to common rotation.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:vortex}
After translating the center of vorticity to the origin, and modulo positive
scaling, rotation, reflection, and permutation, five distinct identical
vortices have exactly five relative-equilibrium shapes: the regular pentagon,
the centered square, the collinear configuration, and the two nonclassical
configurations determined by the two real roots of \eqref{eq:QH}.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:repro}
The ancillary Python script supplied with the paper requires Python~3 and SymPy~1.14.  It generates the resultant and all remainder equations from the definitions rather than reading precomputed coefficients.  Assertions are performed in exact rational arithmetic.  Floating-point evaluation is used only at the end to print the illustrative coordinates \eqref{eq:Eminus}--\eqref{eq:Eplus}.  A successful run ends with the message \texttt{ALL EXACT CHECKS PASSED}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:threepoint}
For arbitrary $u,v,w\in\mathbb C$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:threepoint}
 |(u-v)(v-w)(w-u)|
 \le \frac14\bigl(|u|+|v|+|w|\bigr)^3.
\end{equation}
If the right-hand side is nonzero, equality holds if and only if, after a permutation,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:threepoint-eq}
 u=0,\qquad v=-w,\qquad |v|=|w|.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Regard $u,v,w$ as points $A,B,C$ in the Euclidean plane and put
\[
 a=|v-w|,\qquad b=|w-u|,\qquad c=|u-v|.
\]
Let
\[
 m=\min_{P\in\mathbb C}(PA+PB+PC).
\]
Since the origin is an admissible point,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:m-bound}
 m\le |u|+|v|+|w|.
\end{equation}
We prove
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abc-m}
 abc\le \frac{m^3}{4},
\end{equation}
with equality only when $A,B,C$ are collinear, one of them is the midpoint of the other two, and that midpoint is a minimizer in the definition of $m$.

Suppose first that $A,B,C$ are collinear, with $A$ between $B$ and $C$.  Then $a=b+c$ and $m=a$, whence
\[
 abc=a\,bc\le a\frac{(b+c)^2}{4}=\frac{a^3}{4}=\frac{m^3}{4}.
\]
Equality holds exactly when $b=c$.

Now suppose that the triangle is nondegenerate.  If one angle is at least $120^\circ$, say $\angle A\ge120^\circ$, the geometric median is $A$, so $m=b+c$.  Since $a<b+c$,
\[
 abc<(b+c)bc\le \frac{(b+c)^3}{4}=\frac{m^3}{4}.
\]
It remains to consider the case in which all angles are less than $120^\circ$.  Then the geometric median $F$ lies in the interior and
\[
 \angle AFB=\angle BFC=\angle CFA=120^\circ.
\]
Write
\[
 x=FA,\qquad y=FB,\qquad z=FC,
 \qquad p=x+y+z=m,
\]
and set
\[
 q=xy+yz+zx,\qquad r=xyz.
\]
The cosine rule gives
\[
 a^2=y^2+yz+z^2,\qquad
 b^2=z^2+zx+x^2,\qquad
 c^2=x^2+xy+y^2.
\]
A direct expansion yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fermat-identity}
 a^2b^2c^2=p^2q^2-q^3-p^3r.
\end{equation}
Put $t=q/p^2$ and $\rho=r/p^3$.  Then $0<t\le1/3$, and \eqref{eq:fermat-identity} becomes
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fermat-normal}
 \frac{a^2b^2c^2}{p^6}=t^2(1-t)-\rho.
\end{equation}
If $0<t\le1/4$, then
\[
 t^2(1-t)-\rho\le t^2(1-t)\le \frac{3}{64}<\frac1{16}.
\]
If $1/4\le t\le1/3$, Schur's inequality $p^3+9r\ge4pq$ gives
\[
 \rho\ge\frac{4t-1}{9}.
\]
Hence
\[
 \frac{a^2b^2c^2}{p^6}
 \le g(t):=t^2(1-t)-\frac{4t-1}{9}.
\]
Moreover
\[
 g'(t)=2t-3t^2-\frac49<0,
\]
because $27t^2-18t+4>0$ for every real $t$.  Therefore
\[
 g(t)\le g(1/4)=\frac{3}{64}<\frac1{16}.
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:abc-m} is strict for every nondegenerate triangle.

Combining \eqref{eq:abc-m} with \eqref{eq:m-bound} proves \eqref{eq:threepoint}.  If equality holds and the product is nonzero, the preceding discussion forces the collinear equality case: one point, say $A$, is the midpoint of the other two.  Equality in \eqref{eq:m-bound} then forces the origin itself to be the geometric median, hence $A=0$.  Thus $u=0$ and $v=-w$ with $|v|=|w|$.  The converse is immediate.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:n4}
If $z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4\in\mathbb C$ satisfy
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^4|z_j|^2=4,
\]
then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:n4-main}
 \prod_{1\le i<j\le4}|z_i-z_j|^2\le4^4.
\end{equation}
Equality holds if and only if, after a permutation,
\[
 \{z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4\}
 =\{e^{\mathrm i\theta},\mathrm i e^{\mathrm i\theta},-e^{\mathrm i\theta},-\mathrm i e^{\mathrm i\theta}\}
\]
for some $\theta\in\mathbb R$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Introduce the Hadamard coordinates
\begin{align*}
 s&=\frac{z_1+z_2+z_3+z_4}{2},&
 x&=\frac{z_1+z_2-z_3-z_4}{2},\\
 y&=\frac{z_1-z_2+z_3-z_4}{2},&
 t&=\frac{z_1-z_2-z_3+z_4}{2}.
\end{align*}
The Hadamard matrix divided by $2$ is unitary, and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:n4-parseval}
 |s|^2+|x|^2+|y|^2+|t|^2
 =\sum_{j=1}^4|z_j|^2=4.
\end{equation}
The inverse transformation is
\begin{align*}
 z_1&=\frac{s+x+y+t}{2},&
 z_2&=\frac{s+x-y-t}{2},\\
 z_3&=\frac{s-x+y-t}{2},&
 z_4&=\frac{s-x-y+t}{2}.
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
 z_1-z_2=y+t,&z_1-z_3=x+t,&z_1-z_4=x+y,\\
 z_2-z_3=x-y,&z_2-z_4=x-t,&z_3-z_4=y-t,
\end{array}
\]
and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:n4-factor}
 \prod_{i<j}(z_i-z_j)
 =(x^2-y^2)(x^2-t^2)(y^2-t^2).
\end{equation}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:threepoint} to $u=x^2$, $v=y^2$, and $w=t^2$.  By \eqref{eq:n4-parseval},
\begin{align*}
 \left|\prod_{i<j}(z_i-z_j)\right|
 &\le\frac14\bigl(|x|^2+|y|^2+|t|^2\bigr)^3\\
 &\le\frac14\,4^3=16.
\end{align*}
Squaring gives \eqref{eq:n4-main}.

Suppose equality holds.  Equality in the second inequality above and \eqref{eq:n4-parseval} imply $s=0$.  Equality in Lemma~\ref{lem:threepoint}, after permuting $x,y,t$ if necessary, gives
\[
 x=0,\qquad y^2=-t^2,
 \qquad |y|^2=|t|^2=2.
\]
Thus $y=\pm\mathrm i t$.  If $y=\mathrm i t$, then
\[
 z_2=-z_1,\qquad z_4=-z_3,
 \qquad z_3=\mathrm i z_1,
 \qquad |z_1|=1;
\]
the other sign gives the same square with the opposite orientation.  Hence the four points are the vertices of a unit square centered at the origin.  Conversely such a square has product $4^4$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
